subtopics.title: number sense
subtopics.teaching: Teach number sense through magnitude, place value, factors, multiples, divisibility, estimation, fractions, and flexible representations. Emphasize choosing a useful representation before calculating.
subtopics.worked_example: To compare 7/12 and 5/8, use denominator 24: 14/24 versus 15/24, so 5/8 is larger. An estimate also suggests both are a little above one-half.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: comparing numerators or denominators independently, or trusting an exact calculation without checking whether its magnitude is plausible.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: compare and estimate unfamiliar quantities, switch representations strategically, and justify the result with both calculation and magnitude reasoning.

subtopics.title: arithmetic
subtopics.teaching: Teach multi-step arithmetic with fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios, averages, rates, and unit conversion. Track the base quantity whenever a percentage changes.
subtopics.worked_example: A ₹1,000 item discounted 20% costs ₹800; adding 10% tax to the discounted price gives ₹880, because the tax base is ₹800.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: applying every percentage to the original amount or combining quantities expressed in incompatible units.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: solve multi-step numerical problems accurately, preserve units and percentage bases, and verify results using estimation.

subtopics.title: algebra
subtopics.teaching: Teach algebra as a language for unknown quantities and relationships. Cover expressions, equations, substitution, patterns, and equivalent transformations while preserving equality.
subtopics.worked_example: For 4x-7=21, add 7 to both sides to get 4x=28, then divide by 4 to obtain x=7; substitution confirms 28-7=21.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: performing an operation on only one side or combining unlike algebraic terms as though they were similar.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: translate verbal relationships into algebra, manipulate equations safely, recognize useful patterns, and verify solutions.

subtopics.title: geometry
subtopics.teaching: Teach geometric reasoning through properties of angles, triangles, polygons, circles, perimeter, area, volume, symmetry, and spatial relationships. Choose formulas from the diagram rather than memory alone.
subtopics.worked_example: A rectangle 12 cm by 5 cm has perimeter 34 cm and area 60 cm². The different units and formulas make clear that perimeter measures boundary length while area measures surface.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: substituting a dimension into the wrong formula or confusing perimeter, area, and volume.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: extract relevant measurements from diagrams, select the governing property, calculate accurately, and explain why the result fits the figure.

subtopics.title: advanced problem solving
subtopics.teaching: Teach championship mathematics through invariants, parity, bounds, symmetry, case analysis, backward reasoning, and constructive thinking. Encourage students to reduce the search space before calculating.
subtopics.worked_example: In a puzzle asking whether a target sum can be formed from restricted numbers, parity can immediately rule out impossible cases before any enumeration begins.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: starting exhaustive casework before checking structural constraints, causing unnecessary work or missed cases.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify a decisive invariant, bound, or symmetry, reduce the problem to manageable cases, and justify why the remaining cases are complete.

subtopics.title: physics
subtopics.teaching: Teach physics through measurable quantities, units, forces, motion, energy, heat, light, sound, and electricity. Connect equations to physical meaning and conditions.
subtopics.worked_example: A cyclist traveling 18 km in 1.5 hours has average speed 12 km/h. The unit calculation also checks that the result represents distance divided by time.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: inserting numbers into formulas without checking units, direction, or whether the formula's physical conditions apply.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify the governing physical principle, calculate with consistent units, interpret the result, and test whether it is physically plausible.

subtopics.title: chemistry
subtopics.teaching: Teach chemistry through particles, elements, compounds, mixtures, physical changes, chemical reactions, acids, bases, and conservation of matter. Link observations to particle-level explanations.
subtopics.worked_example: Dissolving salt in water produces a mixture that can be separated by evaporation; no new substance is required for the dissolving step.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: calling every visible change chemical or confusing a compound, whose composition is fixed, with a mixture of substances.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: classify substances and changes, explain observations using particle reasoning, and identify evidence for a chemical reaction.

subtopics.title: biology
subtopics.teaching: Teach biology through cells, body systems, reproduction, heredity, ecosystems, adaptation, and structure-function relationships. Connect individual organisms to larger systems.
subtopics.worked_example: Leaves capture light for photosynthesis while roots absorb water and minerals; the different structures support complementary plant functions.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: memorizing organ names without explaining their functions or treating an ecosystem component in isolation.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: explain biological processes using structure, function, interaction, and environmental context.

subtopics.title: Earth science
subtopics.teaching: Teach Earth science as interacting systems involving rocks, soil, water, atmosphere, weather, climate, landforms, and natural hazards. Use cycles and timescales to connect observations.
subtopics.worked_example: Water can evaporate, condense into clouds, precipitate, and return through runoff or infiltration, linking several parts of one cycle.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: treating weather as identical to climate or describing a cycle as a one-way sequence without recognizing continuous movement of matter.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: connect Earth processes across timescales, interpret observations, and distinguish short-term conditions from long-term patterns.

subtopics.title: scientific reasoning
subtopics.teaching: Teach scientific reasoning through observations, variables, hypotheses, controls, measurements, evidence, uncertainty, and appropriately limited conclusions. Separate correlation from causation.
subtopics.worked_example: To test whether fertilizer affects plant growth, keep plant type, light, soil, and water comparable while varying fertilizer and measuring growth using the same method.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: changing several variables at once or claiming a causal effect from an uncontrolled observation.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: design and critique fair tests, identify evidence quality, and state conclusions that match what the data actually supports.

subtopics.title: reading
subtopics.teaching: Teach close reading through main idea, evidence, inference, sequence, purpose, tone, comparison, and author choices. Treat the passage as the primary evidence source.
subtopics.worked_example: If a passage describes repeated delays followed by a revised timetable and improved punctuality, evidence supports an inference about schedule changes improving reliability.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: selecting an option because it sounds generally sensible when the passage does not support it.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: locate decisive textual evidence, distinguish explicit claims from inference, and reject attractive but unsupported distractors.

subtopics.title: vocabulary
subtopics.teaching: Teach vocabulary through context clues, roots, affixes, synonyms, antonyms, collocations, and shades of meaning. Require the sentence context to determine the intended sense.
subtopics.worked_example: In “The path was arduous, so the hikers rested often,” the consequence suggests arduous means difficult or tiring rather than simply long.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: choosing the most familiar dictionary meaning without checking how the word functions in context.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: infer meaning precisely, compare close alternatives, and use newly learned words accurately in context.

subtopics.title: grammar
subtopics.teaching: Teach sentence structure, agreement, tense, clauses, modifiers, punctuation, and parallelism by identifying the grammatical relationship before applying a rule.
subtopics.worked_example: In “Neither the captain nor the players were ready,” the structure requires attention to the paired subjects and the intended agreement rather than choosing a verb by sound alone.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: applying a remembered grammar rule without identifying the sentence structure or the role of each phrase.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: diagnose and correct errors, explain the governing rule, and construct clear grammatical sentences.

subtopics.title: literature
subtopics.teaching: Teach literary understanding through character, setting, conflict, theme, imagery, figurative language, symbolism, and narrative voice. Support interpretation with textual evidence.
subtopics.worked_example: If a character repeatedly avoids a difficult conversation and the narration describes hesitation, the pattern can support an interpretation of fear or uncertainty.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: treating a personal reaction as the only valid theme or interpreting figurative language literally without contextual evidence.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify literary techniques, compare plausible interpretations, and support conclusions with relevant evidence.

subtopics.title: verbal reasoning
subtopics.teaching: Teach verbal reasoning through analogies, classifications, sentence completion, inference, and precise word relationships. State the relationship before evaluating answer choices.
subtopics.worked_example: In “seed : plant :: egg : chick,” the relation is an early developmental stage leading toward the later organism; the exact options must preserve that relation.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: choosing a loosely associated word instead of one that preserves the precise relationship.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: formulate the underlying relationship, test every plausible option, and reject choices that match only by surface association.

subtopics.title: India
subtopics.teaching: Teach Indian knowledge across geography, polity, history, institutions, science, culture, symbols, and achievements. Distinguish stable facts from information that can change over time.
subtopics.worked_example: A question about the national emblem tests a stable civic fact, whereas a question about a current office-holder requires date-aware verification.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: treating changing facts as permanent or confusing institutions that have similar names but different roles.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: retrieve precise Indian facts, identify whether a fact is time-sensitive, and match the exact institution, place, person, or event requested.

subtopics.title: world
subtopics.teaching: Teach world knowledge through countries, capitals, landmarks, organizations, cultures, geography, science, and global events, connecting facts rather than memorizing isolated pairs.
subtopics.worked_example: The Amazon Basin spans multiple countries and connects questions about South American geography, rivers, climate, and biodiversity.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: confusing a capital with its country, a region with a continent, or a geographic feature with the political unit containing it.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: connect world facts accurately, resolve location relationships, and verify precise names and institutional roles when needed.

subtopics.title: history
subtopics.teaching: Teach history through chronology, causes, consequences, movements, civilizations, inventions, and evidence. Use timelines to test whether proposed causal relationships are historically possible.
subtopics.worked_example: A timeline showing an invention before a later industrial change can support a possible influence, but chronology alone does not prove that it caused the change.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: treating temporal sequence as proof of causation or placing events in the wrong period.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: sequence events, distinguish correlation from supported causation, and explain conclusions using historical evidence.

subtopics.title: geography
subtopics.teaching: Teach geography through maps, physical features, climate, resources, population, regions, scale, and spatial relationships. Combine multiple clues instead of relying on one memorized fact.
subtopics.worked_example: Latitude affects climate, but altitude, ocean currents, relief, and local geography can modify conditions at a particular location.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: assuming one geographic variable determines every local condition or confusing map distance with real-world distance without considering scale.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: interpret spatial evidence, combine geographic factors, and explain regional patterns accurately.

subtopics.title: culture
subtopics.teaching: Teach cultural knowledge through languages, literature, art, music, architecture, food, festivals, traditions, and heritage with regional and historical context. Avoid reducing living cultures to stereotypes.
subtopics.worked_example: A classical dance form can be associated with a particular region and tradition while still having evolved through later practice and interpretation.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: assigning a tradition to the wrong community or treating a diverse culture as a single uniform practice.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify cultural facts precisely, distinguish historical origin from later development, and reason respectfully from context.

subtopics.title: series
subtopics.teaching: Teach number and letter series by identifying the transformation between consecutive terms, testing it across the whole sequence, and checking whether alternating positions follow separate rules.
subtopics.worked_example: In 2, 5, 11, 23, the rule is multiply by 2 and add 1, giving 47 next; verifying each transition is stronger than guessing from the final pair.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: fitting a rule to only two terms or ignoring an alternating pattern.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify a consistent rule, test every transition, and reject rules that require unexplained exceptions.

subtopics.title: analogy
subtopics.teaching: Teach analogies by identifying the precise relation between the first pair before applying it to the second pair. Relations may involve function, part-whole, sequence, degree, or category.
subtopics.worked_example: For “book : read :: song : listen”, the relation is object-to-typical action, not merely two culturally related words.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: choosing an option that is associated with the word but does not preserve the same relationship.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: state the relation explicitly, apply it consistently, and compare all plausible choices.

subtopics.title: logic
subtopics.teaching: Teach logical reasoning through statements, conditions, implications, contradictions, and valid conclusions. Separate what must be true from what could be true.
subtopics.worked_example: If all A are B and no B are C, then no A can be C; the conclusion follows through the two stated relationships.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: reversing an implication or treating a possible conclusion as a necessary one.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: derive only conclusions supported by the premises and identify invalid inferences.

subtopics.title: puzzles
subtopics.teaching: Teach puzzles by translating the story into constraints, tables, diagrams, or ordered cases before making deductions.
subtopics.worked_example: For a seating puzzle, record fixed positions first, then apply adjacency and ordering clues to eliminate impossible arrangements systematically.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: holding too many relationships mentally and making an unsupported placement early.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: formalize constraints, propagate deductions, and prove that the remaining arrangement satisfies every clue.

subtopics.title: non-verbal reasoning
subtopics.teaching: Teach visual reasoning through rotations, reflections, symmetry, odd-one-out patterns, shape transformations, and spatial relationships.
subtopics.worked_example: If a figure is rotated 90° clockwise, track each distinctive corner or mark to determine its new position rather than relying on overall visual similarity.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: confusing rotation with reflection or matching a shape by appearance while ignoring orientation.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: describe the transformation precisely, apply it consistently, and eliminate options using invariant features.

subtopics.title: computing
subtopics.teaching: Teach computing through hardware, software, data, algorithms, operating systems, and networks, focusing on how components work together to solve tasks.
subtopics.worked_example: A word processor uses input devices, memory, processor instructions, storage, and an operating system to turn keystrokes into a saved document.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: treating hardware and software as interchangeable or assuming storage and memory serve the same purpose.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify the role of computing components in an unfamiliar scenario and explain how they cooperate.

subtopics.title: internet
subtopics.teaching: Teach the internet as interconnected networks using addressing, routing, protocols, and services. Distinguish the internet itself from individual web services and apps.
subtopics.worked_example: When a student opens a website, a device sends requests through networks to a server and receives data back; the web is one service built on internet infrastructure.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: treating the internet, web, browser, and search engine as synonyms.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: trace a simple online interaction and distinguish the roles of device, network, protocol, browser, and service.

subtopics.title: AI
subtopics.teaching: Teach AI at an inter-school level through prediction, classification, generation, perception, and decision support, while distinguishing AI from ordinary fixed rules.
subtopics.worked_example: A recommendation system can infer likely interests from interaction patterns, while a fixed menu simply displays predefined choices.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: calling every automated feature AI or assuming an AI output is necessarily correct.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify whether a scenario uses AI, state the task it performs, and explain an appropriate limitation or verification step.

subtopics.title: cyber safety
subtopics.teaching: Teach cyber safety through strong authentication, phishing awareness, software updates, privacy, secure sharing, malware awareness, and safe recovery practices.
subtopics.worked_example: A message claiming an urgent account problem and asking for a password link is a phishing warning sign; verify through the official service instead of following the message.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: trusting a message because it uses familiar logos, urgency, or personal details.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: recognize common attack signals and choose safe actions that protect accounts, devices, and information.

subtopics.title: digital society
subtopics.teaching: Teach digital society through digital identity, accessibility, online behavior, misinformation, platform effects, intellectual property, and responsible technology use.
subtopics.worked_example: A viral post can spread widely before its claim is checked, so responsible participation includes evaluating evidence before forwarding it.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: assuming popularity proves truth or ignoring how digital systems affect people who have different access or needs.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: analyze a digital-life scenario from technical, social, and ethical perspectives and justify responsible behavior.

subtopics.title: science news
subtopics.teaching: Teach science-news awareness by identifying the discovery or mission, organization, evidence, significance, and date, while separating reported findings from headlines or speculation.
subtopics.worked_example: A report about a new space mission should be checked for the mission's objective, agency, launch or milestone date, and what scientists actually measured.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: treating a headline's strongest wording as equivalent to the underlying scientific result.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: extract the key verified facts from a science report and distinguish evidence from promotional or speculative language.

subtopics.title: sports
subtopics.teaching: Build sports awareness through competitions, rules, records, teams, athletes, venues, and major results, with attention to the exact event and year.
subtopics.worked_example: A record belongs to a particular sport, event, category, and date; identifying only the athlete is insufficient when several records are associated with the same person.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: mixing different editions, formats, or event categories when recalling a sports fact.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: answer sports-current-awareness questions using precise event, athlete/team, year, and record qualifiers.

subtopics.title: major events
subtopics.teaching: Teach major-event awareness through who, what, where, when, why, and consequence. Build timelines so similarly named events are not conflated.
subtopics.worked_example: For a major international summit, distinguish the host location, participating leaders or institutions, stated agenda, and resulting announcement rather than treating the event name as the whole fact.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: confusing an announcement date with the event date or repeating an unverified claim about an outcome.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: reconstruct the essential facts of a major event and verify the exact qualifier requested.

subtopics.title: institutions
subtopics.teaching: Teach institutional awareness through purpose, headquarters or location, leadership where relevant, membership, and major functions. Similar names should be separated by mandate.
subtopics.worked_example: Two international organizations may both work on development but have different mandates, membership structures, and responsibilities; the function in the question determines the answer.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: choosing an institution from a familiar name without checking its actual mandate.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: distinguish institutions by function, structure, and role and apply those distinctions to unfamiliar questions.

subtopics.title: fact verification
subtopics.teaching: Teach fact verification as checking a claim against reliable evidence, date, source, wording, and context. Compare independent evidence before accepting a striking claim.
subtopics.worked_example: If a post claims a record was broken, verify the official competition record or authoritative report, confirm the date and category, and check that the number refers to the same event.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: trusting a screenshot, viral post, or repeated claim as proof.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify what evidence a claim requires, verify it using appropriate sources, and reject claims whose qualifiers do not match.

subtopics.title: data reasoning
subtopics.teaching: Teach data reasoning by extracting quantities, units, trends, comparisons, and relationships before drawing conclusions. Tables and charts should be read literally before interpretation.
subtopics.worked_example: If a chart shows enrollment rising from 200 to 260, the increase is 60 students or 30%; the percentage requires dividing by the original 200.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: comparing percentages with different bases or inferring causation from a visible trend alone.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: calculate and interpret data accurately, identify the correct comparison base, and separate observation from inference.

subtopics.title: cross-domain clues
subtopics.teaching: Teach cross-domain clues by combining evidence from different subjects without allowing one clue to override a stronger contradiction. Build a candidate set and eliminate systematically.
subtopics.worked_example: A scenario mentioning a monsoon region, a historical port, and a crop can combine geography, history, and agriculture clues to identify a location more reliably than any one clue alone.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: anchoring on the first recognizable clue and ignoring evidence from another domain.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: integrate clues from multiple disciplines, rank their evidential strength, and justify the final identification.

subtopics.title: integrated scenarios
subtopics.teaching: Teach integrated scenarios by decomposing a real-world situation into scientific, mathematical, language, social, and technological questions before solving each part.
subtopics.worked_example: A school plans a solar installation: students may calculate energy use, interpret weather data, evaluate environmental effects, compare costs, and communicate a recommendation.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: solving one component correctly while ignoring constraints imposed by the rest of the scenario.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: connect multiple subject methods into one coherent solution and explain how each result affects the final decision.

subtopics.title: case analysis
subtopics.teaching: Teach case analysis through context, stakeholders, evidence, alternatives, constraints, and consequences. Require conclusions to be supported by the case rather than by outside assumptions.
subtopics.worked_example: A school considering a digital learning tool should examine cost, accessibility, learning evidence, privacy, teacher workload, and student outcomes before choosing it.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: selecting the most impressive option without weighing evidence, trade-offs, and affected stakeholders.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify the central decision, compare alternatives against explicit criteria, and defend a balanced conclusion.

subtopics.title: championship rounds
subtopics.teaching: Teach championship rounds as mixed-domain challenges requiring rapid identification of the subject principle, disciplined elimination, and a final verification pass.
subtopics.worked_example: A round may move from a number pattern to a science fact and then a data chart; the winning strategy is to reset the reasoning method for each question rather than carry assumptions across subjects.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: spending disproportionate time on one difficult question or using the previous question's reasoning style for a different domain.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: switch methods quickly, preserve accuracy under mixed difficulty, and verify high-risk answers before submission.

subtopics.title: mixed sets
subtopics.teaching: Teach mixed-set practice as deliberate switching among domains, with students first identifying the question type before selecting a method. Track errors by domain rather than only by total score.
subtopics.worked_example: A 10-question set might require algebra, reading inference, science reasoning, and geography; classify each question first, then apply the matching strategy.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: beginning calculations or recall before determining what the question actually tests.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: classify mixed questions quickly, select the correct reasoning tool, and maintain accuracy across subject changes.

subtopics.title: time management
subtopics.teaching: Teach time management through triage: answer high-confidence questions first, mark uncertain items, allocate time according to value and difficulty, and reserve a final checking window.
subtopics.worked_example: In a 30-minute round, spending 8 minutes on one hard puzzle can crowd out several easier questions; a deliberate pass structure protects the total score.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: equating persistence with productivity or repeatedly rereading a question without changing the solving approach.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: plan a time budget, recognize when to move on, and finish with enough time for targeted review.

subtopics.title: elimination
subtopics.teaching: Teach elimination as evidence-based removal of options that violate facts, logic, units, grammar, or the question's exact qualifier. Never eliminate merely because an option feels unfamiliar.
subtopics.worked_example: If a geometry option gives an angle sum other than 180° for a triangle, it can be rejected immediately before comparing the remaining choices.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: eliminating an option because it is uncommon rather than because it contradicts evidence.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: state the specific reason each rejected option fails and use elimination only where the evidence supports it.

subtopics.title: accuracy
subtopics.teaching: Teach accuracy as a process: read qualifiers, calculate carefully, check units, compare with estimates, and distinguish answer selection from explanation. Accuracy is protected by repeatable habits.
subtopics.worked_example: If a percentage calculation gives a result larger than the original quantity when the task describes a discount, an estimate exposes the likely error before submission.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: changing a correct answer during review without new evidence or skipping a final check because the reasoning felt easy.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: apply a consistent verification checklist and correct errors based on evidence rather than anxiety or guesswork.

subtopics.title: final review
subtopics.teaching: Teach final review as targeted verification of boundaries, unanswered items, calculations, copied values, units, and question qualifiers. Review should prioritize high-risk errors rather than rereading everything equally.
subtopics.worked_example: If an answer depends on whether a range is inclusive, revisit that boundary explicitly; a single symbol can change the result.
subtopics.pitfall: Pitfall: spending the entire review time rereading already-certain answers while leaving flagged questions unchecked.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: perform a focused final audit, resolve flagged uncertainties, and submit only after checking the highest-impact error risks.
